scenes.heading: Hook and context · 0:00–0:34
scenes.text: Ever wondered how a chromosome can be copied again and again without losing the genes near its ends? Plenty of your cells keep dividing: in your gut lining and the base layer of your skin, worn-out cells are replaced, and before each division, the DNA is copied. And in typical dividing body cells, the ends of that DNA can get a little shorter with each round of copying.

cues.caption: Copied again and again, genes kept?

scenes.heading: Recall: copied in the S phase of interphase · 0:34–1:04
scenes.text: First, when does that copying happen? When we looked at the cell cycle, we placed DNA replication in the S phase of interphase, before mitosis begins. During the S phase, each chromosome's DNA molecule is copied, and the chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere, still one chromosome, with a telomere at each of its four ends.

scenes.heading: Where the telomere sits, and what it is · 1:22–1:57
scenes.text: Zoom in on one end of one chromatid. Here is its DNA as a simple strip, with two genes near the end. Beyond the last gene comes the telomere: one short DNA sequence, repeated over and over. In humans the repeat is T, T, A, G, G, G. It doesn't code for a protein, so a telomere is repeated, non-coding DNA, sitting between the genes and the very tip.

scenes.heading: Round after round, a shorter end · 1:57–2:30
scenes.text: Now copy this molecule and watch the end. The new copy grows along the old one but stops a little short of the tip, so the daughter molecule's end is shorter. The next round starts from that shorter molecule and stops shorter again. In typical dividing somatic cells, telomeres shorten like this, and what goes is telomere, while both genes are untouched. Some cells maintain their telomeres.

scenes.heading: A thought experiment, and the sentence you write · 2:30–3:09
scenes.text: Now a thought experiment, not a real chromosome: take the telomere away and run the same rounds. The shortening end reaches the gene nearest the tip, and the next daughter molecule would lack part of that gene. Put the telomere back. Picture it as a buffer at the end of the line. The buffer: the telomere, the repeated DNA at the tip. The track behind the buffer: the nearby genes. The buffer takes the loss first; the track stays intact. Written properly: telomeres are repeated non-coding DNA at chromosome ends. In typical dividing somatic cells, shortening during repeated replication initially removes telomeric DNA, protecting nearby genes.

scenes.heading: What I told you, on the end you watched · 3:09–3:37
scenes.text: So here is what I told you, on the end you watched. A telomere is repeated, non-coding DNA at each chromosome end. Replication happens in the S phase of interphase. In our model of a typical dividing somatic cell, the end shortens over successive rounds, initially losing telomeric DNA and keeping the nearby genes intact.

scenes.heading: How it is asked, and the reject card · 3:37–4:16
scenes.text: How is this asked? The command word is outline: keep it short, but keep the link. A cloze on DNA replication had one gap describing repeated sequences at the chromosome ends that let replication happen without losing genes; the answer was telomeres. Multiple-choice questions link more divisions to shorter telomeres, and a telomere becoming too short to a cell possibly stopping division. And the hook? In our model, copying leaves a shorter telomere while the nearby genes remain intact.
